content:
Apple is required to respond to Epic Games' complaint filed with the Brazilian antitrust regulator by Monday. Epic Games accuses Apple of making restrictive interpretations of its obligations under the recent antitrust agreement regarding the App Store in Brazil. Details are as follows.

Background

Two months ago, Apple announced that developers are now allowed to distribute apps through alternative app marketplaces in Brazil.

This change is part of a settlement reached with Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre following a years-long antitrust investigation in Brazil over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple has also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% Core Technology Fee on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. You can click here to learn more about the details of this structure.

Epic Questions Apple's Implementation

According to a report by Brazilian newspaper O Globo today (republished by MacMagazine), Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, accusing Apple of creating "structural, technical, and access barriers" that undermine the practical feasibility of alternative app distribution.

Epic stated that while the new terms in Brazil apply only to iOS apps, the agreement Apple reached with CADE "explicitly covers iPadOS."

Epic also reportedly objected to the so-called "scare screen" pages designed to discourage users from installing apps outside the App Store, and opposed the current installation process, claiming that it requires nine steps — six more than Apple's current implementation in Europe.

According to O Globo, Epic added that Apple's initial installation process in Europe required 15 steps, but after being forced to reduce it to six steps, "the download abandonment rate dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is necessary to calculate fees" and argued that this allows Apple to "monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo reported that CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter at this time.
